title: The Friday Pay Run
summary: A fictional payroll-phishing request develops into evidence of an employee account compromise and possible internal phishing.

roles.name: HR
roles.briefing: Protect employee information, keep payroll moving, support employee trust, verify sensitive requests, and escalate appropriately.

roles.name: IT Helpdesk
roles.briefing: Verify identity, secure accounts, preserve evidence, contain compromise, investigate wider impact, and avoid unnecessary disruption.

rounds.title: The Suspicious Payroll Request
rounds.purpose: Connect a payroll concern with a technical warning before either role has the full picture.
rounds.shared_update: An employee reports an urgent message asking them to confirm payroll information before today's pay run.

role_information.hr: The sender display name looks like a senior HR employee. The message requests personal and bank information. The employee is worried their salary may be delayed.
role_information.it-helpdesk: A password reset was requested for the employee earlier this morning from an unfamiliar browser. No incident has been formally reported. The account remains active.

hr.label: Ask the employee to reply asking what details are needed, while HR checks payroll records.
Contact the employee through a trusted channel, preserve the message, and escalate the concern.
Hold the request until another report confirms whether this is isolated.
Send a quick all-staff warning that payroll messages may be suspicious.

it-helpdesk.label: Reset the password immediately and ask the employee to sign in again.
Verify the employee through an approved channel and review recent account activity.
Wait for HR or the employee to confirm compromise before intervening.
Log it as a routine password-reset ticket and continue normal queue handling.

interaction_rules.result_text: HR and Helpdesk connect the payroll message and reset request early.
The warning raises attention, but the account remains active while people ask what to do.
Both teams act quickly, but the investigation starts with avoidable gaps.

rounds.public_consequence: The report is now being treated as suspicious. The quality of the next step depends on whether HR and Helpdesk combine the employee's concern with the account activity.
rounds.facilitator_note: Strong outcomes preserve the message, verify the employee through trusted channels, and escalate without claiming a fictional policy is official. If participants ask what trusted or approved channels mean, keep the answer generic: use a separate known route rather than replying to the suspicious request. Weaker outcomes are plausible because they protect payroll speed or queue discipline, but they delay the shared picture.
rounds.learning_point: A business request and a technical event can be parts of one incident.
discussion_questions: What would each role have missed without the other role's information?
What makes an urgent payroll request risky even when it looks routine?

rounds.title: Repeated Authentication Prompts
rounds.purpose: Decide how to contain a suspected compromise while supporting the employee and preserving useful records.
rounds.shared_update: The employee says they received several authentication prompts during the morning.

role_information.hr: The employee approved one prompt because they thought it related to payroll. They are embarrassed and worried they caused trouble. Payroll preparation is still in progress.
role_information.it-helpdesk: Several failed sign-ins were followed by one successful sign-in from a new device or location. Active sessions are still present.

hr.label: Reassure the employee, pause sensitive payroll changes for this case, and share a timeline with IT.
Prioritise completing payroll, then revisit the security concern after the deadline.
Ask the employee's manager to confirm whether the request is legitimate before HR acts.
Send a general reminder not to approve unexpected prompts, without naming the employee.

it-helpdesk.label: Revoke active sessions, capture sign-in details, and begin account recovery.
Monitor the account briefly to avoid disrupting payroll unless suspicious activity continues.
Reset the password but leave session and sign-in review for later.
Disable the account until the incident-response path confirms it is safe.

interaction_rules.result_text: HR supports the employee while Helpdesk contains the account and preserves records.
Helpdesk contains the account, but HR is caught by surprise during payroll work.
The teams avoid disruption, but uncertainty remains high.

rounds.public_consequence: The authentication prompts make compromise more likely. Account access, employee support, and payroll handling now need to be coordinated.
rounds.facilitator_note: This round should not punish every disruptive action. Sometimes containment costs continuity. Clarify that pausing sensitive payroll changes for this case is narrower than stopping the whole pay run. The discussion is about sequencing and communication, not finding a magic answer.
rounds.learning_objective: Verify identity before sensitive action; preserve evidence.
rounds.learning_point: Prompt fatigue and urgent business context can combine to create risk.
discussion_questions: How can HR support the employee without implying blame?
When is account disruption justified despite business impact?

rounds.title: Suspicious Mailbox Activity
rounds.purpose: Balance evidence preservation and rapid cleanup when persistence is discovered.
rounds.shared_update: A new mailbox forwarding rule has been discovered on the employee's account.

role_information.hr: Payroll must be completed shortly. Disabling access may interrupt an important workflow. Other HR staff are asking whether normal payroll work should continue.
role_information.it-helpdesk: The forwarding rule sends messages outside the organisation. Recent mailbox activity suggests unauthorised access. The exposure scope is not known yet.

hr.label: Pause only sensitive changes tied to this employee and tell HR staff to verify unusual payroll requests.
Continue payroll normally until IT confirms actual data exposure.
Stop all payroll processing until the mailbox issue is fully understood.
Warn all employees that payroll-related messages may be suspicious.

it-helpdesk.label: Capture details of the rule, remove it, and review mailbox access.
Delete the rule immediately and focus on restoring normal access.
Leave the rule briefly while monitoring to learn more about the activity.
Disable mailbox access while preserving logs and investigating.

interaction_rules.result_text: HR keeps payroll controls targeted while Helpdesk captures and removes the forwarding rule.
Containment is strong, but the organisation feels the operational impact immediately.
The visible problem is removed, but investigation detail is weaker.

rounds.public_consequence: The mailbox rule confirms that the incident is no longer just suspicious. The response now affects payroll continuity and the investigation trail.
rounds.facilitator_note: The strongest path usually captures evidence before removal and keeps HR action targeted. Broad or total pauses can be justified but have trust and continuity costs. If IT considers leaving the rule briefly while monitoring, frame it as a risky trade-off, not as a recommended investigative default.
rounds.learning_objective: Balance containment, evidence, continuity, and trust.
rounds.learning_point: Cleanup is not the same as containment if useful evidence disappears.
discussion_questions: What should be preserved before removing suspicious mailbox artefacts?
How targeted can HR's pause be without leaving payroll exposed?

rounds.title: Wider Organisational Impact
rounds.purpose: Coordinate technical scope and employee communication as the incident spreads.
rounds.shared_update: Another employee reports receiving a similar message from the affected account.

role_information.hr: Employees are asking whether payroll information has been exposed. A rushed all-staff message may create panic, but silence may damage trust.
role_information.it-helpdesk: The compromised account may have sent messages to several internal recipients. The full recipient list is still being investigated. Additional accounts may be at risk.

hr.label: Prepare a targeted employee message with verified facts and escalation instructions.
Send an immediate all-staff warning that payroll messages may be fraudulent.
Wait for IT to confirm the full recipient list before communicating.
Respond only to employees who ask questions, keeping public messaging limited.

it-helpdesk.label: Escalate through the incident process, identify recipients, and prioritise risky follow-up activity.
Add temporary controls to reduce similar messages while investigation continues.
Delay action until logs are complete enough to avoid false positives.
Reset credentials for all potentially affected recipients immediately.

interaction_rules.result_text: Communication and technical scoping support each other.
People are warned and technical controls reduce spread, though noise increases.
The teams avoid false alarms, but the incident has more time to spread.

rounds.public_consequence: The incident is now visible beyond one employee. Communication and technical scoping need to move together.
rounds.facilitator_note: There is no perfect communication timing. The exercise should surface what facts are needed, what can be said safely, and why silence can itself create harm. Ask what trade-off the group is accepting rather than asking for the right answer.
rounds.learning_point: Communication should be timely, factual, and linked to the response process.
discussion_questions: What facts are needed before sending a wider warning?
How can technical scoping and employee communication support each other?

rounds.title: Recovery And Communication
rounds.purpose: Finish recovery while preserving accountability, learning, continuity, and employee trust.
rounds.shared_update: The immediate threat is being contained. The organisation now needs to recover, communicate, and learn from the incident.

role_information.hr: The affected employee needs support. Payroll checks still need confirmation. Wording that blames one person could reduce future reporting.
role_information.it-helpdesk: Unauthorised sessions need confirmation, mailbox rules need final review, and technical actions should be documented.

hr.label: Support the employee, confirm sensitive payroll actions, and prepare a factual update through approved channels.
Keep communication minimal to avoid extending anxiety once the account is contained.
Focus on catching up payroll work and leave incident follow-up to IT.
Schedule a lessons-learned discussion with HR and IT, but delay employee messaging.

it-helpdesk.label: Confirm session revocation, remove persistence, restore secure access, and document actions.
Restore access quickly after password reset and handle documentation later.
Keep access restricted until every related account is reviewed.
Close the ticket once technical indicators are removed.

interaction_rules.result_text: Recovery combines employee support, payroll confidence, secure access, and documentation.
Normal work resumes quickly, but the debrief has gaps.
Recovery is careful, but some disruption continues longer than expected.

rounds.public_consequence: The incident is ending, but the final impression depends on how recovery, documentation, and employee communication are handled.
rounds.facilitator_note: Recovery is a people process as well as a technical process. Strong endings combine secure access restoration, clear records, payroll confidence, and non-blaming communication. Preparing a careful update may slow catch-up work slightly, which is the intended trade-off.
rounds.learning_objective: Balance containment, continuity, evidence, and trust.
rounds.learning_point: A good incident response ends with recovery, documentation, and learning, not just removal of the visible threat.
discussion_questions: What should be documented before calling the incident closed?
How can communication encourage future reporting instead of blame?

final_debrief: Which role had information the other role needed?
Which choices improved one metric while harming another?
Where did the group prioritise speed over certainty?
Where did the group protect evidence before cleanup?
How would participants map the lessons to their organisation's approved reporting, verification, and incident-response procedures?
